where: Section 1, last paragraph of the class C discussion
problem: The text says 'the output is rich in harmonics' immediately after explaining that the tank gives 'a voltage across it [that] is almost a pure sine at f₀'. These two statements contradict each other, and a student can end up believing the sine is not really restored. The harmonic-rich waveform is the transistor current (a narrow pulse train), not the tuned output; the tank suppresses those harmonics, leaving only a small residual.
fix: Replace with: 'Class C works only over a narrow band around f₀. The transistor current is a narrow pulse train rich in harmonics, and only the f₀ component appears as a large sine at the tank; the harmonics are mostly suppressed. Any signal whose energy moves outside that narrow band appears as severe distortion.'

problem: 'Class C and class D both raise efficiency by making the transistor conduct for less time than class A does' gives the wrong reason for class D. A class D device may conduct for most of the cycle; its low loss comes from having almost zero voltage across it while it conducts, not from short conduction time.
fix: Rewrite: 'Class C conducts for less than half a cycle, and class D conducts either fully on or fully off. Both keep the transistor out of the region where it carries high current and high voltage at the same time, so efficiency rises.'

problem: 'a class A stage sits near 25 % to 30 %' quotes an upper figure above the standard maximum. A series-fed class A stage has a maximum ideal efficiency of 25 % (50 % only with transformer coupling), so '30 %' overstates it.
fix: Say: 'a class A stage peaks at about 25 % with a resistive load (up to 50 % with a transformer-coupled load)'.
